title: The First Lamp
order: 1

publishedOn: 2026-10-02

The city of Harrow kept its light on credit. Every lamp on every corner burned
a little flame borrowed from the river, and every flame was written down. Ines
Vale had written them down for eleven years, one line per lamp, in a ledger
bound in green cloth that never left her coat.

She started her round at the north gate an hour before dusk, the way her
mother had, and her mother's father before that. The ladder went over her left
shoulder. The ledger went in the inside pocket, against her ribs, where she
could feel it when she breathed. The striker hung from her belt on a short
chain, so that on cold nights she could find it without looking.

The first lamp was the oldest one in Harrow. It stood at the foot of the gate
on a post of black iron, and its glass had gone the colour of weak tea. Ines
climbed three rungs, opened the little door, and held the striker to the wick.
The river answered the way it always did: a thread of blue that ran up the
post, hesitated at the mouth of the wick, and then caught.

She climbed down and opened the ledger. _North gate, post one. Lit at the
fourth bell. Flame steady._ The pencil was short and the line was neat. She
had written the same words more than four thousand times.

## The count

There were six hundred and twelve lamps in Harrow, and Ines knew all of them.
She knew the one on Chandler Row that sputtered if you lit it before the
baker's oven went cold, and the pair outside the counting house that had to be
lit together or one would sulk. She knew which posts leaned, which doors
stuck, which glass had a crack shaped like a fishhook.

The round took four hours on a good night and six on a bad one. Tonight was a
good night. The wind had dropped, the rain had held off, and the river was
high enough that the flames came up eager. By the time the bells rang the
sixth hour she had lit two hundred and nine lamps and written two hundred and
nine lines, and her hands were warm for the first time that week.

It was on Tanner's Bridge that the count went wrong.

The bridge carried eight lamps, four on each rail. Ines lit the north rail
first, as she always did, then crossed to the south. One, two, three. She
climbed down from the third and turned to the fourth, and there was no fourth.

There was a post. There was a lamp on it, glass clean, door shut. And there
was a flame already inside, small and white and perfectly still.

## A flame that was not hers

Ines stood on the wet stones and looked at it for a long time.

Nobody else lit the lamps of Harrow. That was the whole point of the ledger.
The river lent its fire to one keeper at a time, and the keeper wrote down
what was borrowed so the river could be paid back in the spring. A flame that
was not in the ledger was a debt nobody had agreed to.

She climbed the ladder and opened the door. The flame did not lean toward the
draught the way a river flame would. It did not lean at all. It sat on the
wick like a coin on a table, and when she held her palm over it she felt
nothing, no heat, no pull, only a faint pressure, as if the air above it were
slightly heavier than the air around it.

"Who lit you?" she said, and felt foolish, and said it again anyway.

The flame did not answer. Flames in Harrow did not, as a rule, answer. But
when she took the ledger out of her coat and opened it to the night's page,
the line she had not yet written was already there, in her own hand:

_Tanner's Bridge, south rail, post four. Lit before the keeper. Flame
borrowed -- not from the river._

## Closing the book

She did not remember closing the ledger. She remembered the sound it made, a
soft clap that seemed too loud for the bridge, and the way the white flame
behind the glass seemed to settle, as if it had been waiting for exactly that.

There were four hundred and three lamps left in the round. Ines climbed down,
put the ladder on her shoulder, and walked to the next one, because that was
the job, and because the river did not care what had happened on Tanner's
Bridge. It only cared that the city was lit.

She lit every lamp that night. She wrote every line. At the eleventh bell she
reached the south gate, lit the last post, and sat down on the step of the
gatehouse with the ledger on her knees.

Six hundred and twelve lamps. Six hundred and twelve lines. She counted them
twice, with the pencil, touching each one.

Six hundred and thirteen.

The extra line was at the bottom of the last page, below her signature, where
nothing had ever been written. It said only: _Tomorrow, the bridge again._

Ines read it until the bells rang midnight. Then she put the ledger back in
her coat, against her ribs, where she could feel it when she breathed, and
went home to sleep as well as she could.
